chapters.title: Interpersonal Behaviour and Transactional Analysis
chapters.scope: How people communicate and respond to one another, the skills that make it work, and Eric Berne's transactional analysis.

blocks.title: Interpersonal behaviour and its patterns
blocks.html:
The manager of a public-sector bank branch snaps at a clerk at 10 a.m. By noon the clerk is curt with customers, and two of them complain. How people treat each other at work travels, and it travels both ways.

In plain wordsInterpersonal behaviour is how people talk to, listen to and react to one another.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: interpersonal behaviour is the way people communicate, respond and interact with one another, through verbal and non-verbal communication.

Words are only part of it. Non-verbal signals carry much of the message: tone of voice, body language, gestures and the emotions people show. A "fine" said with folded arms means something else. Interpersonal behaviour shapes teamwork, leadership, conflict resolution and, over time, the organisation's culture.

Four patterns. Who is talking to whom changes what the interaction needs. Take an auto-parts plant in Pune:

PatternCore ideaAt the plant
One-to-oneIndividual interaction; trust and clarity matter.A supervisor coaches one machine operator.
One-to-manyA leader communicates with a group; needs clarity and confidence.The plant head briefs the whole shift on a new safety rule.
Many-to-oneSeveral employees communicate with a superior; needs active listening.Operators bring a joint complaint about overtime to their supervisor.
Many-to-manyTeam interaction; needs collaboration, respect and openness.The shift team works out why rejects rose last week.

Reciprocal influence. A's behaviour influences B, and B's response in turn influences A. The loop can run up or down. Positive behaviour strengthens morale, motivation and cooperation; negative behaviour weakens them. In the bank branch, the clerk's curt replies make customers sharper, which makes the clerk sharper still.

Don't confuse interpersonal with intrapersonal. Intrapersonal processes happen inside one person: self-talk, one's own feelings and perception. Interpersonal behaviour happens between two or more people.

Where it breaks. The four patterns say who is talking to whom, not how well. A single meeting can move through all four in ten minutes. Reciprocal influence also explains why a bad exchange is hard to stop: each side waits for the other to soften first.

In practice. The quickest way to change a negative loop is to change your own response, since that is the half you control. Match the pattern to the message: give criticism one-to-one, and share a decision that affects everyone one-to-many, so all hear the same words.

For exams. Expect a question matching a pattern to what it needs, such as many-to-one with active listening.

blocks.title: Types, determinants and skills
blocks.html:
Two salespeople in an electronics showroom argue during a Diwali sale over who should serve a big customer. The same row can end in a clearer split of work, or in months of not speaking. What decides which?

In plain wordsPeople at work either pull together toward a shared goal, or pull apart because their goals or views differ.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: cooperative behaviour is working toward shared goals with mutual respect and openness; conflicting behaviour arises from differing goals, perceptions or misunderstandings.

TypeWhere it comes fromWhat it brings
CooperativeShared goals, respect and opennessTeamwork, creativity and collaboration
ConflictingDifferent goals, perceptions or misunderstandingsManaged constructively: role clarity, better understanding and innovative solutions

Back to the showroom. The manager hears both sides and splits the floor: one person takes televisions, the other kitchen appliances. The conflict produced role clarity. Ignored, it would have produced two people competing for every customer who walked in.

Six determinants shape how a person behaves toward others:

  • Personality: stable traits, such as being reserved or outgoing.
  • Perception: how a person reads others' actions. A late reply can look like rudeness or like a busy day.
  • Attitudes: settled feelings toward people, the job or the organisation.
  • Values: what a person thinks is right and important.
  • Emotional intelligence: the ability to recognise and manage one's own and others' emotions.
  • Motivation: what a person is trying to achieve in the exchange.

Five skills keep interaction constructive:

  • Positive thinking builds resilience and encourages constructive responses.
  • Mutual trust promotes transparency and open communication.
  • Empathy is understanding others' emotions and perspectives. It differs from sympathy, which is feeling sorry for someone.
  • Courtesy maintains respect and professional decorum.
  • Avoiding ego clashes supports harmony, cooperation and teamwork.

Don't confuse disagreement about the work with disagreement about each other. Conflict over tasks or methods, kept moderate, can improve decisions. Conflict over personalities rarely helps; it drains trust and attention. The showroom row became useful once it was about the floor, not about who was the better salesperson.

Where it breaks. The skills are easy to list and hard to practise under pressure. "Avoiding ego clashes" can slide into avoiding every disagreement, so problems stay hidden. The determinants also act together: a person with high emotional intelligence may still clash when their values are at stake.

For exams. Learn the six determinants and five skills as lists. A favourite statement to judge: "all conflict is harmful". It is false, because conflict managed constructively brings clarity and new solutions.

blocks.title: Transactional analysis: Johari window, ego states and transactions
blocks.html:
A team leader asks, "Has the report been sent?" and gets back, "Why are you always checking on me?" A plain question has turned into a quarrel. Transactional analysis explains how.

In plain wordsTransactional analysis looks at each exchange between two people and asks which part of each person spoke, and which part replied.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: transactional analysis (TA), developed by the psychiatrist Eric Berne, explains interactions through ego states, and is used to improve self-awareness, communication and relationships.

The Johari window is usually taught alongside TA as a map of self-awareness. Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham developed it; the name joins their first names. It sorts what is known about a person by two questions: do I know it, and do others know it?

Johari window areaKnown to selfKnown to othersWhat to do
OpenYesYesBuild trust and transparency
BlindNoYesReduce through feedback
HiddenYesNoReduce through self-disclosure
UnknownNoNoExplore through experience

The goal is to enlarge the open area, for better self-awareness, understanding and trust. A new branch manager who interrupts in meetings, without noticing, has it in her blind area. A colleague's honest word moves it into the open.

Ego states. Berne said each person speaks from one of three ego states, each a consistent set of thoughts, feelings and behaviour.

Ego stateWhat it holdsHow it shows
ParentValues, attitudes and behaviour learned from authority figuresGuiding or critical
AdultLogical, factual, rational processingObjective decisions
ChildEmotional, spontaneous, dependent responsesPlayful or rebellious

Transactions. A transaction is one message and its reply. In a complementary transaction the reply comes from the ego state the sender addressed, so communication flows. In a crossed transaction the reply comes from an unexpected ego state, causing misunderstanding or conflict. In an ulterior transaction two messages travel at once: an apparent social one and a hidden psychological one.

The team leader asked Adult to Adult. "Yes, at four o'clock" would have been complementary. "Why are you always checking on me?" came from the Child, aimed at a Parent the leader never used: a crossed transaction.

Don't confuse the two models. The Johari window comes from Luft and Ingham, not from Berne; it is taught with TA because both aim at self-awareness. And an ego state is not an age or a family role: a 25-year-old can speak from the Parent, and a grandparent from the Child.

Where it breaks. TA grew out of clinical practice rather than controlled research, so its terms are easier to use than to test. Labelling a colleague's reply "Child" can also become a way of dismissing them.

For exams. Expect: which Johari area shrinks through feedback (blind) and which through self-disclosure (hidden); and naming a transaction from a short dialogue.

Go deeper for practitioners

Finer states. TA writers often split the Parent into a Nurturing Parent and a Critical (or Controlling) Parent, and the Child into a Free (or Natural) Child and an Adapted Child. "Take a break, you look tired" is Nurturing Parent; "This is careless work" is Critical Parent.

A decision. Your plant sends a circular: "All staff must strictly ensure timely submission of overtime forms. Repeated lapses will not be tolerated." Submissions fall further, and the union protests. The circular spoke from the Critical Parent and drew an Adapted or rebellious Child reply. An Adult version gives the fact, the reason and the fix: "Forms after Friday miss the payroll run, so overtime is paid a month late. Here is the new drop box." Which version would you send?

Links. The blind area is the case for upward and peer feedback in performance appraisal. Perception, in the personality chapter of this unit, explains why the same words land differently on different people.

blocks.title: Life scripts, life positions, strokes and games
blocks.html:
One officer in a district office meets every new idea with "that won't work here". Another keeps rescuing a junior who never learns. Transactional analysis says such habits follow from how people see themselves and others.

In plain wordsA life script is the story about yourself that you learned as a child and still act out without noticing.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: a life script is a largely unconscious pattern formed in childhood that shapes later decisions, relationships and behaviour.

TA aims to recognise unhelpful patterns, change behaviour and support personal growth. Four tools describe the patterns: life positions, strokes, games and the script itself.

Life positions are a person's basic stance toward self and others. Thomas Harris's book I'm OK – You're OK made the phrase widely known.

Life positionOrientationResultSounds like
I'm OK, you're OKPositive toward self and othersHealthy relationships: the ideal position"Let's work it out together."
I'm OK, you're not OKSuperior, blamingTension and conflict"If they did their jobs, we'd be fine."
I'm not OK, you're OKInferior, submissiveDependency"You decide, you know better."
I'm not OK, you're not OKNegative toward self and othersDisengagement"Nothing here will ever change."

Strokes. A stroke is an act of recognition: a word, a nod, a note. Positive strokes (praise, appreciation) build morale and motivation; negative strokes (criticism, disapproval) may discourage. TA also separates conditional strokes, for what a person does, from unconditional strokes, for who they are. People who get no positive strokes may seek negative ones, since being noticed beats being ignored. Managers should give genuine, specific recognition.

Example. A supervisor in a Nashik packing unit says, "Your line had zero rejects this week, and I noticed you trained the newcomer too." That is a positive, conditional stroke, and it tells the worker exactly what to repeat.

Games. Games are recurring patterns of interaction with hidden motives that lead to predictable, often unhelpful outcomes. Eric Berne described many in Games People Play. In "Yes, but…", a person asks for solutions and then rejects each one: "Yes, but we have no budget." "Yes, but the boss won't agree." The hidden aim is to avoid responsibility, and both sides end up frustrated.

Don't confuse a game with one ulterior transaction. An ulterior transaction is a single exchange with a hidden message. A game is a chain of such exchanges, repeated over time, that ends in the same bad feeling. And in TA a game is not play: nobody enjoys the ending.

Where it breaks. Life positions are a counselling vocabulary, not measured traits; one person can shift position from one setting to another. Naming a colleague's "game" aloud usually makes them defensive rather than aware.

In practice. To stop "Yes, but…", stop supplying answers. Ask, "What would you suggest?" This hands back responsibility. To build an OK–OK climate, make strokes specific and frequent, and criticise the work, not the person.

I'm OK, you're OK.

text: The Kuṟaḷ says friendship is not for laughing together but for stepping in to rebuke a friend who goes wrong. In Johari's terms, a friend's honest feedback shrinks the blind area: what others can see in us that we cannot.
pairings.quote: “Friendship is not for laughing together; it is for stepping in to rebuke when one goes too far.” நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று நட்டல் மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென் றிடித்தற் பொருட்டு. Tirukkuṟaḷ 784

text: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad pictures the self as a rider in a chariot: the body is the chariot, the intellect the charioteer and the mind the reins. A modern reader may see the Adult ego state as the charioteer, steering learned habit and raw feeling. The Upaniṣad describes the self's journey, so this is a reading, not Berne's model.
pairings.quote: “Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins.” आत्मानं रथिनं विद्धि शरीरं रथमेव तु । बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च । ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu, buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca. Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3

text: Kabir advises keeping a critic close, even housing him in your courtyard, because he cleans your nature without soap or water. The Johari window says the blind area, what others see in us and we do not, shrinks only through feedback. Both treat criticism from others as the way to see yourself.
pairings.quote: “Keep your critic close; give him a hut in your courtyard. Without water, without soap, he makes your nature clean.” निन्दक नियरे राखिये, आंगन कुटी छवाय । बिन पानी साबुन बिना, निरमल करे सुभाय ॥ nindak niyare rākhiye, āṅgan kuṭī chhavāy; bin pānī sābun binā, nirmal kare subhāy. Kabīr, sākhī (Hindi)

chapters.title: Organisational Culture and Climate
chapters.scope: The shared meaning that makes one organisation unlike another, how it is built and kept, and how it feels to work there.

blocks.title: What organisational culture is
blocks.html:
Two private banks in the same city sell the same products at similar rates. In one, a clerk who spots an error tells the manager at once; in the other, she keeps quiet. No rule book explains the difference.

In plain wordsCulture is "the way we do things here": the values and habits people in an organisation share, often without saying them.

Exam definitionOrganisational culture is a system of shared meaning held by members that distinguishes the organisation from other organisations (Robbins and Judge).

Culture is made of shared values, beliefs and norms. It shapes how things are done there, and new members pick it up mostly by watching.

Three levels. Edgar Schein showed that culture sits at different depths. What you can see on a visit is only the top layer.

In the first bank, the artefact might be an "error of the week" board. The espoused value is "we own our mistakes". The basic assumption, never written down, is that reporting an error will not cost you your job. That last layer is why the clerk speaks up.

Seven characteristics. Robbins and Judge list seven characteristics that, taken together, capture an organisation's culture. Each runs from low to high, so a culture is a profile across all seven.

DimensionWhat it measures
Innovation and risk-takingExperimentation, creativity, willingness to take risks
Attention to detailPrecision, analysis, thoroughness
Outcome orientationResults, performance, achieving targets
People orientationThe effect of decisions on employees and their well-being
Team orientationCollaboration and collective achievement
AggressivenessCompetitiveness and assertiveness
StabilityOrder, consistency, keeping the status quo

For illustration: a young software firm in Bengaluru might score high on innovation and outcomes and low on stability. A long-established insurance office might show the reverse profile. Neither is wrong; each fits different work.

Don't confuse culture with the rule book. Policies are written and official. Culture is what people actually do. When the two disagree, people usually follow the culture.

Where it breaks. The seven characteristics describe a culture; they do not say which culture is best. That depends on the work and the strategy. Culture is also hard to measure: surveys pick up espoused values far more easily than the assumptions underneath.

For exams. Learn the Robbins and Judge definition word for word, the seven characteristics, and Schein's three levels in order: artefacts, espoused values, basic assumptions.

blocks.title: Strength and functions of culture
blocks.html:
In a family-run chain of sweet shops, every new hire hears the founder's rule on day one: never sell yesterday's sweets. Years later, staff still throw out unsold stock with no manager watching. That is what a strong culture looks like.

In plain wordsA culture is strong when most people hold the same core values, and hold them firmly.

Exam definitionIn a strong culture, the organisation's core values are both intensely held and widely shared (Robbins and Judge).

Dominant culture and subcultures. A dominant culture is the core values most members accept, often shaped by founders and top management. Subcultures are smaller cultures within departments, locations or professions. They combine the organisation's values with local experience.

Example: in a pharmaceutical company, the sales team prizes speed and targets, while the quality-control lab prizes caution. Both still share the company's core value of patient safety. That shared core is the dominant culture; the two styles are subcultures.

FeatureStrong cultureWeak culture
Looks likeShared beliefs, clear norms, common goalsFragmented beliefs, inconsistent messages
Leads toLoyalty, engagement and consistent behaviourLess unity, weaker values, disconnected employees

What culture does. Culture does five jobs for an organisation:

FunctionWhat culture does
Boundary definitionDistinguishes the organisation from others
IdentityGives members a sense of belonging
CommitmentConnects employees to a shared mission
StabilityActs as social glue holding the organisation together
Behaviour guideSignals what is acceptable, even without formal rules

The behaviour-guide function is why the sweet-shop staff need no supervisor. A strong culture works like an unwritten rule book, so the organisation needs fewer written rules.

Don't confuse a strong culture with a good one. Strength measures how widely and firmly values are held, not whether they are the right values. A culture can be strongly committed to hiding bad news.

Where it breaks. Strength cuts both ways. A strong culture can become a barrier to change when the market moves. It can push out people who think differently, working against diversity. And two strong cultures often clash after a merger.

For exams. Expect the five functions as a matching question, especially "social glue" (stability). Know that subcultures sit inside a dominant culture, not against it.

Boundary, identity, commitment, stability, guide.

blocks.title: How culture is built and kept
blocks.html:
A founder who answered every customer complaint personally sells his firm twenty years later. Staff still answer complaints within the day. Nobody wrote that down; it was built in, and then kept alive.

In plain wordsSocialisation is how a newcomer learns "how things are done here" and becomes an insider.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: socialisation is the process that adapts new employees to the organisation's culture.

Who builds it. Culture starts with the founder's philosophy, whose values shape hiring, leadership style and expectations. Top management keeps it alive as role models, through their decisions and behaviour. Reinforcement mechanisms strengthen it: selection, training, performance evaluation, rewards and promotion.

How newcomers learn it. Socialisation runs in three stages. Follow a new probationary officer joining a public-sector bank:

Socialisation stageWhat happensThe new officer
Pre-arrivalExpectations form before joining, through interviews, websites and reviews.Hears from seniors and coaching classes what branch life is like.
EncounterExpectations meet reality through orientation, onboarding and practice.Finds the first rural branch busier and more paper-bound than expected.
MetamorphosisThe employee adapts and fits into the organisation's norms.Learns the unwritten rules and starts teaching them to the next batch.

When metamorphosis goes well, the newcomer becomes more productive and committed, and is less likely to leave.

A positive culture builds on employees' strengths rather than dwelling on weaknesses. It rewards more than it punishes, and supports growth through learning, creativity and career development. Its limit: positivity does not remove the need for objective standards and constructive feedback.

Don't confuse socialisation with training. Training teaches the skills of the job: how to process a loan. Socialisation teaches the norms: whether you may question the manager's decision on it.

Where it breaks. A founder's influence fades as a firm grows and hires people who never met them. Hiring for "fit" keeps the culture strong, but it can shut out people with different backgrounds and ideas. Reinforcement only works if the rewards match the stated values.

For exams. Know the three socialisation stages in order, and the five reinforcement mechanisms.

Go deeper for practitioners

What leaders really teach. Edgar Schein argued that people learn a culture from what leaders do, not what they announce. Staff watch what leaders pay attention to and measure, how they react in a crisis, and how they spend money. They also watch whom leaders reward, hire and promote.

A decision. You head a regional sales office. The company's stated value is "customer first", but bonuses are paid only on monthly volume. Staff push stock onto dealers at month-end, and returns follow. A poster campaign about customers will not change this. Changing what the bonus counts, for example adding dealer returns to the calculation, will. Which lever do you pull first?

Links. Selection and training appear in the recruitment and training chapters of this unit. Their cultural role is often bigger than their formal one.

Pre-arrival, encounter, metamorphosis.

blocks.title: Types of culture, and climate
blocks.html:
A government office has the same rules and values it had for decades. Then a harsh new head arrives, and within a month people stop speaking up in meetings. The culture has not changed; the climate has.

In plain wordsClimate is how it feels to work somewhere right now.

Exam definitionA standard textbook definition: organisational climate is the shared perception members have of their organisation and work environment.

Four types of culture. Kim Cameron and Robert Quinn's competing values framework sorts cultures by two questions. Does the organisation look inward, at its own people and processes, or outward, at customers and competitors? And does it prize flexibility or stability?

TypeCharacterValues
Clan (collaborate)Warm, family-likeMentoring, teamwork, involvement
Adhocracy (create)Dynamic, entrepreneurialInnovation, risk-taking, adaptability
Market (compete)Competitive, results-drivenGoals, performance, measurable outcomes
Hierarchy (control)Structured, rule-basedStability, order, formal procedures

For illustration: a small family business in Surat may run like a clan, a start-up like an adhocracy, a sales-driven consumer firm like a market, and a district treasury like a hierarchy.

Climate. Climate can be people-oriented (well-being and morale), rule-oriented (policies and procedures), innovation-oriented (creativity and new ideas) or goal-oriented (targets and performance).

AspectCultureClimate
FocusShared values and meaningsShared perceptions and feelings
NatureDeep-rooted, relatively stableMore immediate and changeable
TimeLong-termCurrent experience
Core question“How do we do things here?”“What does it feel like to work here?”

Don't confuse culture with climate. Culture is the deep layer of values that takes years to shift. Climate is the surface feel that one manager can change in a month, as in the government office above.

Where it breaks. Few organisations are pure types; most mix two or more, and departments differ. The framework's point is the tension between corners, such as control against creativity. A climate survey is also a snapshot: it can swing with one bad quarter.

In practice. A manager cannot change the culture alone, but can change the climate of a team quickly. How you react to the first piece of bad news you hear sets it.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. A clan-like family firm is bought by a market-type group. The new owners bring monthly targets and league tables. Long-serving staff feel the warmth has gone, and two senior people resign. The buyer can keep the targets and protect what the clan valued, such as mentoring, by building it into managers' goals. Or it can expect the culture to adjust on its own. Which costs more if it fails?

Opposite corners. In the framework, clan sits opposite market, and adhocracy opposite hierarchy. Moves between opposite corners are the hardest, because the values directly conflict.

Culture is values and meaning; climate is perceptions and feelings.

text: Kauṭilya opens his chapter on the ruler's duties by observing that when the ruler is active his servants become active too, and when he is careless they grow careless and eat into his work. Culture theory says the same of founders and top managers: their conduct becomes the standard.
pairings.quote: “When the ruler is active, his servants rise with him; when he is careless, they are careless too.” राजानमुत्थितमनूत्तिष्ठन्ते भृत्याः । प्रमाद्यन्तमनुप्रमाद्यन्ति । rājānam utthitam anūttiṣṭhante bhṛtyāḥ; pramādyantam anupramādyanti. Arthaśāstra 1.19.1–2

pairings.classic: where the mind is without fear
text: Tagore's poem asks for a place where the mind is without fear, the head held high and knowledge free. A people-oriented or innovation-oriented climate rests on the same conditions: people speak up when they are not afraid, and ideas move when knowledge is shared. Tagore was praying for a country, so the comparison is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; where knowledge is free.” চিত্ত যেথা ভয়শূন্য, উচ্চ যেথা শির, জ্ঞান যেথা মুক্ত chitto jetha bhoyshunyo, uchcho jetha shir, gyan jetha mukto Rabindranath Tagore, Naivedya 72 (Bengali, 1901); his English in Gitanjali 35

chapters.title: Workforce Diversity and Cross-Cultural Behaviour
chapters.scope: Recognising and respecting differences at work, managing them fairly, and working well across national cultures.

blocks.title: Workforce diversity and its dimensions
blocks.html:
Workforce diversity is recognising and respecting differences among employees in age, gender, race, religion, ethnicity, physical ability and background. Diversity is more than tolerance: it means inclusion, equal opportunity and respect. Its benefits include innovation, creativity, balanced decisions, harmony and efficiency.

Managing diversity means creating a workplace where everyone can perform fairly and without bias, through fairness and equity (equal opportunity), inclusion (valuing different identities), respect (preventing discrimination and exclusion) and a business link (performance and competitiveness).

DimensionWhat it calls for
Race and ethnicityRespect for cultural heritage and traditions; equality at work
Age and generationUnderstanding different values, expectations and ways of communicating
Gender and identityInclusion of all gender identities
Sexual orientationA safe, discrimination-free environment and equal rights
Religious beliefsFlexible schedules, attire and prayer facilities
DisabilityAssistive tools, accessibility and ability-focused roles
Socioeconomic backgroundDiverse perspectives and equal opportunity

blocks.title: Techniques for managing diversity
blocks.html:
TechniqueHow
Raising awarenessTraining, storytelling, discussion
Shared cultureCross-cultural collaboration
Special care programmesFlexible work, accessibility, wellness
Career developmentMentoring, training, promotion
Ending discriminationAddressing hidden bias and the glass ceiling
Preventing sexual harassmentZero tolerance and safe reporting
Diverse committeesSeveral perspectives in decisions

Diversity also plays out in groups: formal groups (organisational tasks, such as an HR team), informal groups (personal relationships, such as a lunch group), and in-groups and out-groups, which create belonging for some and exclusion for others. Members take task roles (the planner), relationship roles (the motivator) or individual roles (the dominator).

blocks.title: Cross-cultural behaviour and Hofstede
blocks.html:
Cross-cultural organisational behaviour studies how cultural differences affect behaviour in multicultural workplaces. Globalisation brings multicultural workplaces and cultural differences, and with them the need to adapt. Done well, it brings adaptation to cultural norms, better international HR strategies, better cooperation, fewer misunderstandings and greater global competitiveness.

Hofstede's dimensionHighLow
Power distanceHierarchy and authority acceptedEquality and informality
Uncertainty avoidanceStructure and risk avoidance (France)Flexibility and openness (Singapore)
Individualism and collectivismSelf-reliance (the United States)Group orientation (India)
Masculinity and femininityCompetition and assertiveness (Japan)Cooperation and quality of life (Sweden)
Time orientationLong-term persistence (China)Short-term results (the United States)

P, U, I, M, T: power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individualism, masculinity, time orientation.

blocks.title: Culture shock and cross-cultural training
blocks.html:
Culture shock is the set of difficulties a person faces in adapting to an unfamiliar culture. Its causes include language barriers, new customs and emotional stress. It is reduced by training, then adjustment support, then integration.

Training areaAim
Self-awarenessUnderstand one's own cultural assumptions
Host-country knowledgeCustoms and workplace practices
Role clarificationResponsibilities and expectations
Intercultural communicationEffective communication across cultures
Conflict resolutionHandling cultural misunderstandings

text: A Ṛgvedic hymn says that what is real is one, and the wise speak of it in many ways. Read for the workplace, it treats differences of expression as compatible with a shared core, the premise of inclusion rather than mere tolerance. The hymn is about naming the divine, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Truth is one; the wise call it by many names.” एकं सद्विप्रा बहुधा वदन्ति । ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti. Ṛgveda 1.164.46

text: A verse found in the Mahā Upaniṣad, with a close variant in the Hitopadeśa and the Pañcatantra, says that only the narrow-minded count people as kin and not kin; for the large-hearted, the whole world is one family. In-groups and out-groups are exactly that counting.
pairings.quote: “‘This one is kin, that one is not’ is the reckoning of the small-minded; for those of noble conduct, the whole earth is a family.” अयं बन्धुरयं नेति गणना लघुचेतसाम् । उदारचरितानां तु वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम् । ayaṃ bandhur ayaṃ neti gaṇanā laghucetasām, udāracaritānāṃ tu vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam. Mahā Upaniṣad 6.71

pairings.classic: the customs of regions and guilds
text: Manu tells the ruler, in settling matters, to take account of the customs of castes, of regions, of guilds and of families. Guilds (śreṇī) were the trade associations of the time, so this is an early instruction to recognise each group's own norms and give effect to them, which is what cross-cultural management asks.
pairings.quote: जातिजानपदान्धर्मान्श्रेणीधर्मांश्च धर्मवित् । समीक्ष्य कुलधर्मांश्च स्वधर्मं प्रतिपादयेत् । jāti-jānapadān dharmān śreṇī-dharmāṃś ca dharmavit, samīkṣya kula-dharmāṃś ca sva-dharmaṃ pratipādayet. “One who knows the law should examine the customs of castes, regions, guilds and families, and then establish the law particular to each.” Manusmṛti 8.41

pairings.classic: one caste, one religion, one God
text: Narayana Guru's best-known saying, one caste, one religion, one God for humankind, was a challenge to caste division in Kerala. Diversity management also rejects exclusion, but it goes about it differently: it names differences in order to respect them, where the Guru said the dividing lines had no basis.
pairings.quote: “One caste, one religion, one God for humankind.” ഒരു ജാതി, ഒരു മതം, ഒരു ദൈവം മനുഷ്യന് oru jāti, oru matam, oru daivam manuṣyanŭ. Śrī Nārāyaṇa Guru (Malayalam)

chapters.title: Emotions and Stress Management
chapters.scope: Emotions, moods and emotional intelligence at work, and the causes, effects and management of work stress.

blocks.title: Emotions, moods and affect
blocks.html:
Affect is the broad emotional background of positive and negative feelings: a person's overall emotional tone. Emotions are brief, intense and specific feelings directed at a person or event, such as joy, anger or fear; they trigger quick reactions and influence motivation and decisions. Moods are general, longer-lasting states, often without a definite cause, that colour perception and behaviour over time.

NatureDurationTrigger
EmotionSpecific, intenseShortA particular event or person
MoodGeneral, mildLongOften unknown
AffectBroad emotional toneVariesOverall emotional state

Emotions drive behaviour, influence decisions, prepare the body for action and shape how we read social situations. They may be universal, but display rules vary across cultures, and understanding the differences reduces misunderstanding at work. Six emotions are widely treated as universal: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust. Descartes named six primitive passions: wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness.

blocks.title: Sources of emotions and moods
blocks.html:
SourceEffect
PersonalitySets baseline emotional tendencies.
WeatherEffects are generally limited; a link people perceive may be an illusion of correlation.
StressPersistent demands without relief can trigger negative emotions.
Social interactionPositive contact can lift mood; isolation or conflict may lower it.
SleepPoor sleep weakens emotional regulation: irritability and poorer judgement.
ExerciseHelps improve mood and reduce tension.
AgeEmotional regulation may improve with age and experience.
SexPatterns of expression may differ between men and women, but individual and cultural variation is substantial.

blocks.title: Emotional labour and emotional intelligence
blocks.html:
Emotional labour is managing and displaying the emotions a job requires, which may differ from what the employee actually feels; a customer-service employee stays cheerful while feeling stressed. Emotional dissonance is the gap between felt and displayed emotion. Prolonged, it can lead to fatigue, burnout and job dissatisfaction. Empathy and emotional awareness help manage these demands.

Emotional intelligence (EI) is the ability to recognise, understand and manage one's own emotions and those of others.

ComponentWhat it does
Self-awarenessRecognise your own emotions
Emotional regulationManage your emotional responses
EmpathyUnderstand others
RelationshipsImprove interaction and teamwork

People with high EI tend to stay calm under stress, manage conflict, stay motivated and optimistic, make balanced decisions and work well in teams.

blocks.title: Work stress
blocks.html:
Stress occurs when important demands stretch a person's capacity to cope. Common triggers are excessive pressure, unclear roles and an imbalance between demands and resources: when resources match or exceed demands, stress is lower; when demands exceed resources, the result is strain.

Challenge stressors (deadlines, demanding projects) can energise and motivate. Hindrance stressors (bureaucracy, workplace conflict) get in the way of goals.

SourceExamples
EnvironmentalPolitical instability, economic uncertainty, technological change
OrganisationalHeavy workload, poor management, role ambiguity, conflict
PersonalFamily or financial problems, personality, perfectionism

Small stressors accumulate and can become overwhelming. The consequences are physiological (raised heart rate, headaches, fatigue), psychological (anxiety, mood changes, depression, low satisfaction) and behavioural (absenteeism, lower performance, withdrawal, substance abuse).

Moderate stress may enhance performance; chronic stress brings burnout, illness and decline.

blocks.title: Stress management
blocks.html:
Stress is managed from two sides at once.

Individual approachesOrganisational approaches
Time management: prioritise, organise, cut distractionsSelection and job fit: match skills with roles
Physical exercise: relieve tension, improve energyTraining and development: build competence, reduce anxiety
Relaxation: meditation, deep breathing, mindfulnessClear goal setting: specific goals and feedback
Social support: emotional comfort, advice, copingJob redesign, empowerment and better communication
Sabbaticals and wellness programmes

text: The Gītā's portrait of a person of steady wisdom: undisturbed in sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger. Emotional regulation aims at a similar steadiness, though emotional intelligence also values recognising emotions, not only rising above them.
pairings.quote: “Undisturbed in sorrow, free of craving in pleasure, without attachment, fear or anger: such a person is called steady in wisdom.” दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः । वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते । duḥkheṣv anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣu vigata-spṛhaḥ, vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīr munir ucyate. Bhagavad Gītā 2.56

pairings.classic: seeing others' joy and sorrow as one's own
text: The Gītā praises the person who, measuring by themselves, sees the joy and sorrow of others as equal to their own. That is empathy, one of the four parts of emotional intelligence.
pairings.quote: “Who, by comparison with themself, sees the joy and sorrow of all beings as their own is held to be the highest yogin.” आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन । सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं स योगी परमो मतः । ātmaupamyena sarvatra samaṃ paśyati yo ’rjuna, sukhaṃ vā yadi vā duḥkhaṃ sa yogī paramo mataḥ. Bhagavad Gītā 6.32

text: The Kuṟaḷ says the best course is to bear with those who scorn you, as the earth bears those who dig into it. Emotional labour asks something similar of a service employee facing a rude customer. The modern view adds a warning the couplet does not give: a long gap between what is felt and what is shown leads to burnout.
pairings.quote: “As the earth bears those who dig into it, so to bear with those who scorn you is best.” அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 151

pairings.classic: moderation in food, rest and sleep
text: The Gītā says discipline removes sorrow for one who is moderate in eating and recreation, measured in effort at work, and regular in sleep and waking. Exercise, rest and time management, the individual approaches to stress, are that same moderation.
pairings.quote: “For one moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, and regular in sleep and waking, discipline destroys sorrow.” युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु । युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा । yuktāhāra-vihārasya yukta-ceṣṭasya karmasu, yukta-svapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkha-hā. Bhagavad Gītā 6.17

text: Śāntideva gives a two-line test for distress: if something can be remedied, dismay is unnecessary; if it cannot, dismay does not help. That is the split stress research makes between problem-focused coping, acting on what can be changed, and managing one's response to what cannot.
pairings.quote: “If there is a remedy, what use is dismay? And if there is no remedy, what use is dismay?” यद्यस्त्येव प्रतीकारो दौर्मनस्येन तत्र किम् । अथ नास्ति प्रतीकारो दौर्मनस्येन तत्र किम् । yady asty eva pratīkāro daurmanasyena tatra kim, atha nāsti pratīkāro daurmanasyena tatra kim. གལ་ཏེ་བཅོས་སུ་ཡོད་ན་ནི། །དེ་ལ་མི་དགར་ཅི་ཞིག་ཡོད། །གལ་ཏེ་བཅོས་སུ་མེད་ན་ནི། །དེ་ལ་མི་དགའ་བྱས་ཅི་ཕན། ། gal te bcos su yod na ni, de la mi dgar ci zhig yod, gal te bcos su med na ni, de la mi dga' byas ci phan. Śāntideva, Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.10 (Sanskrit; Tibetan in the Derge Tengyur, Toh 3871)

chapters.title: Organisational Justice and Whistleblowing
chapters.scope: Whether people see their workplace as fair in outcomes, processes and treatment, and how wrongdoing can be reported safely.

blocks.title: Organisational justice
blocks.html:
Two officers at a public-sector bank branch get the same pay rise. One hears it from the manager, with the reasons. The other learns it from a payslip, along with a rumour that a colleague lobbied for more. The rupees match; the sense of fairness does not.

In plain wordsOrganisational justice is how fair people feel their workplace is: what they get, how it was decided, and how they were treated along the way.

Exam definitionOrganisational justice is employees' perception of fairness in the workplace. It covers both the outcome a person receives and how that outcome is reached and communicated. Jerald Greenberg popularised the term in 1987.

The key word is perception. Justice here means what employees believe, not what management intended. A rule that managers think is fair still fails if staff believe it is rigged.

It matters because fairness builds trust, trust builds morale, morale builds productivity, and all of it helps the organisation keep its people.

DimensionThe question it asksAt the bank branch
DistributiveWas the outcome fair?Was my rise fair, compared with what others got for similar work?
ProceduralWas the process fair?Were rises decided by known rules, or by who lobbied hardest?
InteractionalWas I treated fairly?Did anyone explain the decision to me, and with respect?

Don't confuse justice with getting what you want. People often accept a disappointing outcome when the process and the treatment were fair. They can also feel wronged by a good outcome that was decided in secret or delivered with contempt.

Where it breaks. Perceptions differ. The same decision can seem fair to one employee and unfair to the next, depending on whom each compares themselves with. Researchers also disagree on how to divide justice up: some fold interactional justice into procedural justice, and others split it in two.

In practice. When staff say a decision is "unfair", find out which of the three they mean. A pay structure, an appeals route and a manager's manner need different fixes.

For exams. Remember Greenberg (1987), and match each dimension to its question: outcome, process, treatment.

Outcome, process, treatment.

blocks.title: Distributive and procedural justice
blocks.html:
A college fest committee has ₹1 lakh left over to thank its 20 volunteers. Split it equally, pay by hours worked, or help the students who spent their own money on travel? Each choice is defensible, and each will strike someone as unfair.

In plain wordsDistributive justice asks whether the shares were fair. Procedural justice asks whether the way of deciding was fair.

Exam definitionDistributive justice is the perceived fairness of how outcomes are allocated: pay, promotions, recognition, workloads and resources. Procedural justice is the perceived fairness of the methods used to reach decisions, even when the outcome is unfavourable.

Distributive justice. Three principles can govern the sharing.

PrincipleRewards are based onAt the fest committee (an illustration)
EquityContribution or inputThe volunteers logged 1,000 hours in all. One who worked 60 hours gets 60 ÷ 1,000 of ₹1 lakh = ₹6,000.
EqualityAn equal share for everyone₹1 lakh ÷ 20 = ₹5,000 each.
NeedIndividual needsFirst repay the students who paid their own travel; share the rest.

The equity principle rests on J. Stacy Adams's equity theory. People compare the ratio of what they get to what they put in with the same ratio for others. Morton Deutsch (1975) argued that the right principle depends on the goal. Equity suits a group aiming at productivity, equality suits one aiming at harmony, and need suits one caring for welfare.

Procedural justice. Gerald Leventhal (1980) set out six rules a fair procedure should follow. Take promotions to branch manager in a bank.

RuleMeaningIn a promotion decision
ConsistencyThe same rules for everyone, every timeEvery candidate takes the same test and interview
Freedom from biasNo prejudice or favouritismNo panel member assesses a relative
AccuracyReliable, adequate informationThe panel uses the whole year's record, not last month's
RepresentationEmployees have a voiceCandidates can present their own case
CorrectabilityA way to challenge or appealAn unsuccessful candidate can appeal to a higher committee
EthicalityMoral and legal standards upheldScores stay confidential; no rule or law is bent

Don't confuse equity with equality. Equity pays in proportion to contribution, so shares differ. Equality gives everyone the same share, whatever each contributed.

Where it breaks. The three distribution principles conflict, and people favour whichever helps them. Equity also needs contribution that can be measured. In close teamwork it often cannot, and an equity rule then rewards whoever is most visible.

For exams. Expect matching questions: equity, equality and need to their bases, and each of the six rules to its meaning. Correctability (appeal) and representation (voice) are the pair most often swapped.

Go deeper for practitioners

The fair-process effect. People accept unfavourable outcomes more readily when they believe the process was fair. John Thibaut and Laurens Walker (1975) traced much of this to voice: the chance to state one's case, even when someone else decides.

Which kind of justice predicts what. Many studies find that distributive justice is linked mainly with reactions to the outcome itself, such as satisfaction with pay. Procedural justice is linked more with attitudes to the organisation, such as commitment and trust in management. Jason Colquitt (2001) showed that a four-part model fits the evidence best: distributive, procedural, interpersonal and informational justice.

A decision. An auto-parts plant in Pune moves from equal shift bonuses to bonuses tied to each line's output. The fastest lines welcome it; the line with the oldest machine protests. The distributive change may be defensible. The protest is likely to fade only if the procedure looks fair too: the measure is explained, machine downtime is excluded, and supervisors can appeal a wrong figure.

C, B, A, R, C, E: consistency, bias-free, accuracy, representation, correctability, ethicality.

blocks.title: Interactional justice
blocks.html:
A bank cancels one region's Diwali bonus because targets were missed. One branch manager gathers her team, shows the figures and answers questions. Another sends a one-line email. The loss is the same; the anger is not.

In plain wordsInteractional justice is being treated with respect, and being told the truth, when decisions about you are made.

Exam definitionInteractional justice is the perceived fairness of the treatment people receive when procedures are carried out and decisions are communicated. Robert Bies and Joseph Moag introduced the idea in 1986.

It has two parts.

PartWhat it requiresIn the bonus example
Interpersonal justiceDignity, respect and courtesyThe manager tells the team in person, listens, and does not blame or mock anyone
Informational justiceExplanations that are honest, timely and adequateShe explains why the bonus was cut, shows the figures, says what would bring it back, and does this before the rumours start

Put together with the other two dimensions, the picture is complete.

Kind of justiceConcerns
DistributiveThe outcome
ProceduralThe process
InteractionalThe treatment

Don't confuse interactional justice with procedural justice. Procedural justice concerns the rules of the process, which are designed in advance. Interactional justice concerns how the person carrying them out behaves. A fair procedure can still be delivered rudely or without explanation.

Where it breaks. Respectful delivery helps people accept a hard decision; it does not make an unfair decision fair. Courtesy repeated over decisions that keep going against the same people soon sounds hollow. Researchers also debate whether this is a separate dimension or part of procedural justice. Jason Colquitt (2001) treated its two parts as two separate dimensions.

In practice. When giving bad news, say it early and in person. Give the real reason and what happens next, then listen. Each step costs nothing, and each one is a test of interactional justice.

For exams. Interpersonal is about dignity; informational is about explanation. Both sit under interactional justice.

Respect in treatment, honesty in explanation.

blocks.title: Whistleblowing
blocks.html:
An accounts executive notices that one supplier's invoices are paid twice every month. Her manager tells her to leave it alone. What she does next, and whom she tells, is the subject of whistleblowing.

In plain wordsWhistleblowing is when someone inside or close to an organisation reports wrongdoing to people who can stop it.

Exam definitionWhistleblowing is the disclosure by organisation members (former or current) of illegal, immoral or illegitimate practices under the control of their employers, to persons or organisations that may be able to effect action (Janet Near and Marcia Miceli, 1985).

Its purpose is to protect ethical, legal and public interests. Common concerns are fraud, financial manipulation, bribery and corruption, unsafe conditions, discrimination, insider trading and other unethical acts.

Who reports. Employees, customers and clients, contractors, consultants, vendors and suppliers may all report. What they risk. Whistleblowers face retaliation: career setbacks, legal threats, social ostracism and harassment.

FeatureInternal whistleblowingExternal whistleblowing
Reported toHR, senior management, an ethics committeeRegulators, legal authorities, the media
WhenGenerally the preferred first step, giving the organisation a chance to actWhen internal mechanisms fail or the environment is hostile

Don't confuse whistleblowing with a personal grievance. A grievance is about the complainant's own treatment, such as pay or a transfer. Whistleblowing is about wrongdoing that harms others, the organisation or the public.

Where it breaks. A reporting channel works only if people trust it. If reports go to the person involved, or nothing visibly happens, people stay silent. Anonymous reports protect the reporter but can be hard to investigate. Some reports turn out to be mistaken.

In practice. A useful internal channel offers more than one route, so a report can bypass the line manager. It keeps the reporter's identity confidential, protects against retaliation, and tells the reporter what was done.

For exams. Know the Near and Miceli definition, the internal–external distinction, and the forms retaliation takes.

Go deeper for practitioners

A decision. Back to the accounts executive. Going straight to the media would skip the organisation's chance to act and expose her to the most risk. Staying silent leaves the fraud running. The usual path is to write down what she found, with dates and amounts. She then reports it through a channel that bypasses her manager, such as the head of finance, internal audit or an ethics committee. She goes outside only if that fails.

For the manager who receives a report. Thank the person, keep their identity limited to those who must know, and investigate without warning the people involved. Then tell the reporter, in general terms, that action was taken. How the first few reports are handled decides whether anyone makes a second one.

Links. Whistleblowing turns on the same trust as organisational justice: people report when they expect a fair process and fair treatment. Business ethics and CSR (Unit 1) covers the wider duties involved.

Wrongdoing, then internal reporting, then resolution; if unresolved or hostile, external reporting.

blocks.title: Reportable offences, benefits and India's framework
blocks.html:
A board that learns of a fraud from a newspaper has lost twice: once to the fraud, and again to the headline. A working reporting channel might have brought it to light years earlier, when it was smaller.

What can be reported. Reportable offences fall into a few groups.

GroupOffences
Breaking rulesLegal, contractual and ethical violations; intellectual property violations
Money and dataFinancial or data fraud; misuse of property or funds
Harm to people and placesHealth and safety risks; environmental violations
PowerAbuse of power

Why it helps the organisation. Whistleblowing brings early detection of legal and operational risks. It builds trust among employees, customers and investors, supports an ethical culture and a responsible public image, prevents major scandals, and adds transparency. Take a hypothetical case: a supplier who double-bills ₹2 lakh a month has taken ₹24 lakh in a year. A report in the first month stops it at ₹2 lakh.

India's framework.

IndiaWhat it provides
Companies Act, 2013Mechanisms for inspecting a company's affairs; the Serious Fraud Investigation Office for serious fraud; vigil mechanisms required of specified companies.
SEBI frameworkWhistleblower mechanisms in listed entities, with avenues and safeguards for reporting.
Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014A framework for receiving public-interest disclosures about corruption or misuse of power by public servants, and for protecting those who make them against victimisation. Enacted, but not yet brought into force.

False or malicious complaints may attract penalties under the applicable law.

Don't confuse the 2014 Act with the corporate rules. The Whistle Blowers Protection Act concerns disclosures about public servants, and it has not yet been brought into force. Vigil mechanisms in companies come from the Companies Act, 2013, and those in listed entities from the SEBI framework.

Where it breaks. A vigil mechanism on paper does not help if staff doubt that reports are kept confidential or acted on. And because the 2014 Act has not been brought into force, its protections cannot yet be relied on.

In practice. Managers should know where their organisation's vigil mechanism is, who receives reports, and how a report bypasses the line manager. Staff should be able to answer the same questions.

For exams. Match each law to what it provides. Remember that the Serious Fraud Investigation Office comes under the Companies Act, 2013. The 2014 Act is enacted but not in force.

text: The Kuṟaḷ calls it the ornament of the wise to be like a balance that weighs evenly and leans to neither side. Organisational justice is that impartiality, as employees perceive it.
pairings.quote: “Like a balance that weighs evenly, leaning to neither side: such impartiality is the ornament of the wise.” சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் அமைந்தொருபால் கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி. Tirukkuṟaḷ 118

text: The Kuṟaḷ says that when a ruler does not treat everyone alike but regards each according to their worth, many will live by that regard. Distributive justice by equity, reward in line with contribution, is the same principle.
pairings.quote: “If the ruler does not regard all alike but each by their worth, many will live by that regard.” பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின் அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர். Tirukkuṟaḷ 528

text: Justice, says the Kuṟaḷ, is to examine carefully, show favour to no one, and act impartially toward all after weighing the matter. Procedural justice sets out the same requirements: accuracy, freedom from bias and consistency.
pairings.quote: “To inquire, to favour none, to act impartially toward all after weighing the matter: that is justice.” ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடா திறைபுரிந் தியார்மாட்டும் தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை. Tirukkuṟaḷ 541

text: The Kuṟaḷ compares speaking harshly when kind words are at hand to picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit is there. Interactional justice asks that decisions, even hard ones, be delivered with dignity, respect and courtesy.
pairings.quote: “To speak harshly when kind words are at hand is to pick the unripe fruit when the ripe is there.” இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல் கனியிருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந் தற்று. Tirukkuṟaḷ 100

pairings.classic: a ruler who can be reached
text: Kauṭilya warns the ruler not to keep people with business waiting at his door: a ruler who is hard to reach is made, by those around him, to confuse what should and should not be done. Internal reporting channels serve a similar purpose in a company, a way for bad news to reach the top past the inner circle. Kauṭilya is writing about petitions to a king, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: Arthaśāstra 1.19

pairings.classic: do not despise, do not belittle
text: Basavanna's vacana lists what not to do: steal, kill, lie, rage, despise others, praise yourself, belittle the person in front of you, and calls this purity inside and out. Interpersonal justice asks for dignity, respect and courtesy in how people are treated. The vacana is a personal code, so the link is a reading.
pairings.quote: “Do not steal, do not kill, do not lie, do not rage, do not despise others, do not praise yourself, do not belittle the one before you. This is inner purity; this is outer purity.” ಕಳಬೇಡ, ಕೊಲಬೇಡ, ಹುಸಿಯ ನುಡಿಯಲು ಬೇಡ, ಮುನಿಯ ಬೇಡ, ಅನ್ಯರಿಗೆ ಅಸಹ್ಯಪಡಬೇಡ, ತನ್ನ ಬಣ್ಣಿಸಬೇಡ, ಇದಿರ ಹಳಿಯಲು ಬೇಡ. ಇದೇ ಅಂತರಂಗಶುದ್ಧಿ, ಇದೇ ಬಹಿರಂಗಶುದ್ಧಿ. kaḷabēḍa, kolabēḍa, husiya nuḍiyalu bēḍa, muniya bēḍa, anyarige asahyapaḍabēḍa, tanna baṇṇisabēḍa, idira haḷiyalu bēḍa. idē antaraṅgaśuddhi, idē bahiraṅgaśuddhi. Basavaṇṇa, vacana (Kannada)

chapters.title: Human Resource Management
chapters.scope: What HRM is, how it grew, what it aims at and does, and how it differs from personnel management and from organisational behaviour.

blocks.title: Meaning and objectives of HRM
blocks.html:
Human resource management (HRM) is the process of acquiring, developing, motivating and retaining employees to achieve organisational goals. It aims to maximise performance, ensure employee welfare and align people with the organisation's strategy.

Acquire → Develop → Motivate → Retain: a skilled, motivated and committed workforce
ObjectivesExamples
PersonalTraining, career development, work-life balance, satisfaction
OrganisationalProductivity, performance, workforce planning, talent management
OtherLegal compliance, social responsibility, diversity and inclusion, fairness

blocks.html:

text: The Kuṟaḷ's rule for assigning work: having judged that this person will accomplish this task by these means, leave the task to them. Acquiring and developing a workforce turns that judgement into a system.
